difficultyReason: Two-move argument: the historian first undermines a general claim with a counterexample, then advances an alternative explanation. The correct answer must capture both moves; traps describe only one.
stimulus: Historian: Many scholars maintain that the printing press was the principal cause of the Reformation's rapid spread across Europe. But the Waldensian movement spread widely across the same regions three centuries earlier, entirely by hand-copied manuscripts and itinerant preachers. A better explanation for the Reformation's reach, then, is the dense network of lay preachers already connecting parishes long before any press was built.

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing a historical case that conflicts with a widely accepted explanation and then proposing a different explanation in its place

choices.label: B
choices.text: arguing that because two phenomena share a feature, they must share a cause

choices.label: C
choices.text: rejecting an explanation solely on the ground that its proponents have a vested interest in defending it

choices.label: D
choices.text: showing that an explanation is self-contradictory and therefore cannot be true

choices.label: E
choices.text: appealing to expert consensus in order to settle a disputed historical question

explanations.correct: The historian invokes the Waldensian movement as a counterexample that undercuts the printing-press explanation, then offers the preacher-network as an alternative. A captures both moves.
explanations.B: No shared-feature-to-shared-cause inference is made; the Waldensian case is used against an explanation, not to infer causal identity.
explanations.C: The historian never attacks the motives of the scholars, only their explanation.
explanations.D: The printing-press explanation is shown to be insufficient, not internally contradictory.
explanations.E: No expert consensus is cited; the historian pushes back against the prevailing view.

difficultyReason: The physician both questions whether the reported data actually support a causal claim and offers a competing mechanism. Traps describe only the critique or only the alternative.
stimulus:
Columnist: A recent study reports that adults who take a daily multivitamin have fewer colds per year than those who do not, and concludes that the multivitamin strengthens the immune response.
Physician: The study surveyed only people who already took multivitamins voluntarily. Such people also tend to exercise, sleep more regularly, and eat more fresh produce. The apparent benefit is more plausibly attributed to those habits than to the vitamin itself.
questionStem: The physician responds to the columnist by

choices.label: A
choices.text: identifying a feature of the study's sample that undermines its causal conclusion and offering an alternative explanation for the reported correlation

choices.label: B
choices.text: arguing that the study's authors have falsified their data in order to promote a product

choices.label: C
choices.text: denying that any correlation between multivitamin use and cold frequency exists

choices.label: D
choices.text: showing that the columnist's conclusion rests on an ambiguous definition of 'immune response'

choices.label: E
choices.text: generalizing from personal clinical experience to reject a finding supported by quantitative research

explanations.correct: The physician points to a sampling problem (self-selection) that weakens the causal claim and then supplies a rival cause. Both moves are captured by A.
explanations.B: No accusation of fabrication is made.
explanations.C: The correlation itself is accepted; what is challenged is the causal reading.
explanations.D: No ambiguity in terminology is raised.
explanations.E: The physician cites patterns in the study population, not personal clinical anecdotes.

difficultyReason: The ethicist uses a hypothetical variant to show that an opposing principle produces an unacceptable verdict, then endorses a rival principle. Traps isolate only the hypothetical or only the endorsement.
stimulus: Ethicist: Some argue that any act done to produce a greater overall good is thereby justified. But suppose a surgeon could save five patients by harvesting the organs of one unwilling donor who walked into the clinic. Few would accept that the surgeon acts rightly. A more adequate principle, then, is that even acts that maximize good are impermissible when they treat a person merely as a resource.

choices.label: A
choices.text: presenting a hypothetical case whose implications conflict with one principle and offering a revised principle that better accommodates them

choices.label: B
choices.text: defending a familiar moral principle by deducing it from more basic axioms

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy between medical ethics and ordinary commercial transactions

choices.label: D
choices.text: citing statistical evidence about public attitudes toward organ donation

choices.label: E
choices.text: claiming that a principle is false because it is not universally followed

explanations.correct: The surgeon hypothetical functions as a counterexample to the maximizing-good principle; the ethicist then proposes a revised principle. A captures this combined maneuver.
explanations.B: There is no deduction from more basic axioms; the argument is driven by a counterexample.
explanations.C: No analogy with commerce is drawn.
explanations.D: No statistics are invoked; the ethicist appeals to what 'few would accept,' not polling data.
explanations.E: The principle is rejected as producing wrong verdicts, not as being unfollowed in practice.

difficultyReason: The economist both denies a causal inference drawn from a correlation and supplies a mechanism that fits the data equally well. Traps describe only the denial or only the alternative.
stimulus: Economist: Commentators frequently claim that minimum-wage increases cause long-term unemployment among teenagers, pointing to the fact that teenage joblessness has risen in several states shortly after such increases. But teenage labor-force participation in those same states declined as school enrollment grew, which on its own would raise measured unemployment. The rise in joblessness is better explained by shifting educational patterns than by the wage policy.
questionStem: The economist's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: challenges a causal claim about an observed trend by identifying a separate factor that would produce the same trend

choices.label: B
choices.text: concedes that a policy had the effects attributed to it, but argues that those effects were worth the cost

choices.label: C
choices.text: appeals to a general economic principle and applies it to a specific policy question

choices.label: D
choices.text: argues that because a policy has one beneficial effect, it must have no harmful effects

choices.label: E
choices.text: attacks a conclusion by questioning the credentials of those who proposed it

explanations.correct: The economist concedes the rise in joblessness but denies the causal link to minimum-wage policy by pointing to a confounding factor (enrollment-driven drops in participation) that would yield the same statistic. A captures this technique.
explanations.B: No concession about minimum-wage effects is made; the economist denies those effects.
explanations.C: No general principle is cited or applied; the argument works through a specific competing cause.
explanations.D: The economist does not argue that minimum-wage policy is wholly benign.

difficultyReason: The law professor first distinguishes two kinds of cases, then applies the distinction to defeat a proposed rule. Traps describe only the distinction or only the conclusion.
stimulus: Law professor: It is sometimes said that judges should never rely on unpublished decisions. But a judge may rely on an unpublished decision either as binding precedent or merely as persuasive reasoning. When treated as binding, the decision controls outcomes other courts have never had a chance to scrutinize; when treated as persuasive, it is simply one more source of argument. So the blanket prohibition is unwarranted: only reliance of the first kind raises the concerns critics actually cite.
questionStem: The law professor's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: drawing a distinction between two uses of a practice and arguing that the objection to the practice applies only to one of them

choices.label: B
choices.text: showing that a proposed rule would produce an outcome the critics themselves would condemn

choices.label: C
choices.text: rejecting a rule on the ground that it has never been adopted in any jurisdiction

choices.label: D
choices.text: identifying an ambiguity in a legal term and concluding that the term should be abandoned

choices.label: E
choices.text: appealing to an analogy between legal practice and scientific experimentation

explanations.correct: The professor separates 'binding' from 'persuasive' reliance, then argues the critics' worry applies only to the first, so a blanket ban is too broad. A captures both moves.
explanations.B: No reductio targeting critics is developed; the professor analyzes the critics' concern rather than turning it on them.
explanations.D: The term 'unpublished decision' is not treated as ambiguous; two ways of relying on it are distinguished.
explanations.E: No analogy to science is made.

difficultyReason: The ecologist concedes a premise of the opposing view but argues it does not support the recommended conclusion, and then proposes a different policy consistent with the same evidence.
stimulus: Ecologist: Conservationists urge that, since the population of the spotted salamander has fallen sharply across the region, logging in the adjacent forest should be halted. It is true that the population has fallen. But the decline tracks almost perfectly with the loss of breeding pools well away from logging sites. Limiting logging would do little for the salamander; restoring those pools would do a great deal more.
questionStem: The ecologist's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: accepts the factual claim on which an argument is based but denies that it supports the recommended policy, and advances a different policy better supported by the same evidence

choices.label: B
choices.text: disputes the reliability of data cited by an opponent and proposes collecting better data before any policy is set

choices.label: C
choices.text: argues that a proposed policy, though well-intentioned, would actually accelerate the problem it aims to solve

choices.label: D
choices.text: concludes that because two policies address the same problem, both should be implemented simultaneously

choices.label: E
choices.text: derives a general principle about species decline from a single local case

explanations.correct: The ecologist grants the decline but denies that logging restrictions are warranted by it, substituting pool restoration. A captures concede-then-redirect.
explanations.B: The population data are accepted, not impugned.
explanations.C: There is no claim that halting logging would worsen matters.
explanations.D: The argument rejects one policy in favor of another, not both.
explanations.E: No general principle about species decline is offered; the reasoning is specific to this case.

difficultyReason: The engineer rejects an analogy as misleading and replaces it with a more apt one. Traps isolate one half of the move or invert the direction.
stimulus: Engineer: Critics compare self-driving cars to commercial aircraft, claiming that, since aviation autopilot has had decades to mature, self-driving systems will require equally long timelines before they are safe. But aircraft operate in sparse, highly regulated airspace, while cars share crowded roads with unpredictable human drivers. A closer comparison is to industrial robotics, where machines learned to work safely alongside people only through extensive real-world co-operation, not merely through internal refinement.

choices.label: A
choices.text: rejecting a comparison on the basis of a relevant dissimilarity and substituting a different comparison that the engineer regards as more apt

choices.label: B
choices.text: arguing that because two technologies share a feature, predictions about one apply to the other

choices.label: C
choices.text: claiming that critics of self-driving cars have a financial stake in delaying their deployment

choices.label: D
choices.text: using a mathematical model of risk to establish a precise timeline

choices.label: E
choices.text: conceding that self-driving cars are unsafe and arguing that they should be banned

explanations.correct: The engineer points out that aviation and driving environments differ in ways that break the analogy, then proposes industrial robotics as a better match. A captures the replace-analogy technique.
explanations.B: The argument denies that aviation and cars share the relevant features; it does not transfer predictions on that basis.
explanations.E: The engineer implies self-driving cars can become safe, not that they should be banned.

difficultyReason: The linguist disputes a definition-based claim by producing a counterexample and then offers a refined criterion. Both moves must be captured; traps name only one.
stimulus: Linguist: Some grammarians define a 'pidgin' as any simplified language formed from contact between speakers of different tongues. On that definition, the contact variety used by sign-language interpreters would count as a pidgin, yet it plainly is not. What distinguishes a pidgin is not simplification but the lack of native speakers for whom it is a first language.

choices.label: A
choices.text: offering a case that a proposed definition wrongly classifies and then introducing a different criterion that avoids the misclassification

choices.label: B
choices.text: arguing that because a term is used loosely in everyday speech, it should not be defined at all

choices.label: C
choices.text: establishing a general claim about language change from a single example

choices.label: D
choices.text: showing that two definitions of a term are logically equivalent

choices.label: E
choices.text: conceding a definition but arguing that it applies to fewer cases than its proponents claim

explanations.correct: The interpreter example is offered as a misclassified case under the simplification-based definition; the linguist then supplies the native-speaker criterion. A captures both moves.
explanations.B: The argument does not say the term should go undefined; it offers a better definition.
explanations.C: No general claim about language change is drawn.
explanations.D: Two definitions are contrasted, not shown to be equivalent.
explanations.E: The original definition is rejected as wrong, not accepted with narrower scope.

difficultyReason: The curator critiques a general aesthetic principle by showing a valued work would be excluded under it, then reformulates the principle. Traps describe only the reductio-like move or only the reformulation.
stimulus: Curator: The dean argues that, because good art must reward close visual attention, the museum should collect only figurative painting. But the best works of mid-century color-field abstraction reward prolonged attention every bit as fully as figurative works, and excluding them would impoverish our collection. The dean's principle is sound in its emphasis on sustained attention, but it should be framed in terms of rewarding attention, not in terms of depicting recognizable subjects.

choices.label: A
choices.text: arguing that a proposed criterion would exclude works it ought to include, and then restating the criterion in a way that covers them

choices.label: B
choices.text: defending one school of painting by attacking the artistic credentials of another

choices.label: C
choices.text: showing that the dean's principle rests on a false historical claim about mid-century art

choices.label: D
choices.text: arguing that aesthetic principles cannot be formulated in general terms

choices.label: E
choices.text: deriving a new principle by combining two principles already accepted by the dean

explanations.correct: The curator shows that figurative-only collecting would wrongly exclude color-field works, then reframes the principle around sustained attention rather than recognizable subjects. A captures both moves.
explanations.B: The curator does not attack figurative painting's credentials; it argues for a broader inclusion.
explanations.C: No historical falsehood is alleged against the dean.
explanations.D: The curator offers a revised general principle, not a rejection of general principles.
explanations.E: Only one principle is in play, not a combination of two.

difficultyReason: The analyst undermines a policy recommendation by showing its premise does not fit the relevant population, and then identifies a subgroup for which a different recommendation would follow.
stimulus: Policy analyst: The mayor proposes free citywide transit on the ground that free transit in several small towns has increased ridership and cut car use. But those towns had little car traffic to begin with; residents walked or biked for most trips. In a dense city where most commuters already drive long distances, free transit is unlikely to pull drivers out of their cars. If the aim is reducing car use, congestion pricing in the downtown core, where driving is a real choice rather than a necessity, is a better lever.

choices.label: A
choices.text: arguing that evidence supporting a proposal does not transfer to the relevant setting, and advocating a different measure targeted at conditions in that setting

choices.label: B
choices.text: conceding that free transit would reduce car use, but arguing that it would cost more than the city can afford

choices.label: C
choices.text: appealing to the preferences of a majority of residents to reject a mayoral proposal

choices.label: D
choices.text: assuming that because a policy has worked in one large city, it will work in any large city

choices.label: E
choices.text: arguing that a policy should be judged solely by whether it eliminates car use entirely

explanations.correct: The analyst argues that the small-town evidence fails to apply to a dense, car-dependent city, and then advocates congestion pricing in the relevant subsetting. A captures the transferability critique plus targeted alternative.
explanations.B: Cost is never mentioned; transferability of effects is the issue.
explanations.C: No appeal to majority preferences is made.
explanations.D: The analyst denies a generalization across settings rather than relying on one.
explanations.E: The analyst treats 'reducing car use' as the aim, not 'eliminating' it.
